passage: My name is Noor, and for two years I only went to my professor when I was drowning. I would ask, get an answer, mumble thanks and vanish. Then the professor said at the end of one meeting, "Let me know how it goes." I noticed that I never had. So this time I fixed the errors and the next day sent a short message: "Thank you for Tuesday. Your tip about the boundary condition fixed the whole second section." Two weeks later I brought a new draft and a fresh question. The professor remembered the earlier one. I had always thought asking for help was a single favour. It turned out to be the start of a conversation.

Research log – S. Kale, Monday
Abhinav, a third-year, came to office hours two weeks ago with a regression model that kept giving strange results. We found the issue in fifteen minutes: two of his variables measured almost the same thing.
That same evening, he emailed: 'Thank you, sir. I removed one of the two variables and the results now make sense. The error went from 18% to 6%.' Short, specific, and he had clearly done the work.
Today he came back with a new version and one new question, about whether to include rainfall data. I noticed I was pleased to see him. It is not a one-time favour anymore; I know his project now and can help more quickly each time.
I have told him about the department's summer research list. I think he should apply.

qa.q: What happened to the error after Abhinav removed one variable?
What might Abhinav have felt sending the thank-you with specific results?
qa.a: Abhinav likely felt grateful and proud, wanting to show that the professor's help was actually used.

qa.q: What should Abhinav do after hearing about the summer research list?
qa.a: Apply, and keep sending short progress updates, so the relationship grows around real work.

qa.q: How does S. Kale feel seeing Abhinav return?
qa.a: S. Kale is pleased and more invested, since the thank-you and new work turned a single favour into an ongoing relationship.

grounding: Shows a student sending a short, specific thank-you after a professor's help and returning with new work, turning one favour into a lasting relationship.

passage:
Thursday
Three weeks ago I sat in Dr Dolma Bhutia's office completely stuck on my botany project: my seedlings kept dying and I didn't know why. She looked at my photos and said, 'Your soil stays too wet. Drill holes in the cups.' That was it. Ten minutes.
I almost didn't write to thank her. It felt like bothering her twice. But Didi said a thank-you costs nothing. So that night I wrote: 'Thank you, ma'am. I drilled holes in all 30 cups. 27 seedlings are alive this week, compared with 11 before.'
Today I went back with my growth graph and one new question, about light hours. She smiled as soon as I walked in and said, 'Ah, the seedling person.' She remembered my project! We talked for twenty minutes, and she lent me a book.
I think this is what people mean by a mentor.
– Lalit

qa.q: How many seedlings were alive after the holes were drilled?
qa.a: 27 seedlings are alive this week, compared with 11 before.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about writing the thank-you at first?
qa.a: Lalit felt hesitant, worried it would be bothering the professor twice, until Didi's advice.

qa.q: What could Lalit do to keep the connection going?
qa.a: Return the book with a short note on what was learned, and share the next graph when the light experiment ends.

qa.q: How might Dr Bhutia feel when Lalit walks in again?
qa.a: She is happy and engaged, remembering the project, since the thank-you with results showed her advice worked.

grounding: Shows a student sending thanks with specific results after a professor's help and returning with new work, which grows into mentorship.
